Lublin Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Lublin, Poland

Not demolished. Lublin held conventions of the Waad Arba Aracot (Council of Four Lands), the supreme Jewish self-governing body of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth documented at several other towns in this collection, and was a center of Hebrew printing from the 16th through 18th centuries. Jews were forbidden to live within the city walls from the late 15th century, settling instead in surrounding jurisdictions; the city became an important Hasidic center from the end of the 18th century, and the interwar period saw the operation of the world-famous Chachmei Lublin Yeshiva, one of pre-WWII Europe's most prestigious institutions of Jewish learning. By 1865, Jews formed a majority of the city, 59 percent of its population. Following the WWII destruction of the Podzamcze district and the 1941–42 deportation of ghetto Jews to Majdanek and Bełżec, a small Jewish community nonetheless survives in Lublin today, operating since 1993 as a branch of the Warsaw Jewish community. This cemetery, likely established in the first quarter of the 14th century on Grodzisko hill, functioned until 1831 in part because a second layer of soil was periodically added to extend its capacity. Over 200 matzevot survive, including 14 from the 16th century — the oldest dated 1541, among the earliest tombstones documented anywhere in this collection — commemorating eminent scholars, marshals of the Waad Arba Aracot, and famous rabbis.
